```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(heumilkr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggExtra)

result <- readRDS("perf.rds")

rho_mean <- round(100 * mean(result$clarke_wright_perf_rho), 1)
xi_mean <- round(100 * mean(result$clarke_wright_perf_xi), 1)

description <-
  data.frame(
    group = c("A", "B", "E", "F", "tai", "X", "Loggi", "ORTEC"),
    group_desc = c(
      "Augerat A, 1995", "Augerat B, 1995",
      "Christofides and Eilon, 1969", "Fisher, 1994",
      "Rochat and Taillard, 1995", "Uchoa et al., 2017",
      "Loggi (DIMACS, 2021)", "ORTEC (DIMACS, 2021)"
    )
  )

real <- result[result$group %in% c("Loggi", "ORTEC"), ]
rho_real_mean <- round(100 * mean(real$clarke_wright_perf_rho), 1)

runtime_ms <- function(data) {
  round(1000 * max(data$runtime), 0)
}
large <- result[result$n_site == max(result$n_site), ]
```

In this vignette we discuss performance benchmarks of the Clarke-Wright algorithm implemented in this package by comparing the Clarke-Wright solutions of a set of problem instances with their best known value, and by measuring the run time on those instances.

### The problem instance data

The problem instances we are basing our measurements on are provided courtesy of [CVRPLIB](https://galgos.inf.puc-rio.br/cvrplib/en/instances) and can be divided into eight groups[^1] of different characteristics:

[^1]: The naming is directly taken from [CVRPLIB](https://galgos.inf.puc-rio.br/cvrplib/en/instances)

-   Augerat A, 1995 (27 instances)

-   Augerat B, 1995 (23 instances)

-   Christofides and Eilon, 1969 (13 instances)

-   Fisher, 1994 (3 instances)

-   Rochat and Taillard, 1995 (12 instances)

-   Uchoa et al., 2017 (100 generated instances with 100 to 1000 sites)

-   Loggi, DIMACS 2021 (6 instances with 400 to 1000 sites, extracted from real problems)

-   ORTEC, DIMACS 2021 (6 instances with 241 to 700 sites, derived from real problems)

The data provides the problem instance as well as the best known solution, whose cost is available as the field `best_known_cost` of each instance. CVRPLIB lists the best known solutions of all instances of the first five groups as proven optimal, but only for 61 of the 100 instances by Uchoa et al. and for none of the Loggi and ORTEC instances. For those, a better solution than the best known one might exist.

The data of the first five groups is bundled with this package. The results for all groups are precomputed, so that building this vignette does not require downloading anything. See `data-raw/perf.R` in the [package source](https://github.com/lschneiderbauer/heumilkr) for how they are obtained.

## Relation to best known and trivial solution

The idea of this indicator is to measure where the Clarke-Wright solution sits in between the best known solution and the trivial solution[^2]. Let $\gamma$ be the cost of the Clarke-Wright solution, $\omega$ the cost of the best known solution, and $\alpha$ the cost of the trivial solution. The measure $\xi$ is defined to be $$\xi := 1 - \frac{\gamma - \omega}{\alpha - \omega}\,.$$ The measure can move between zero and 1. It is zero if the solution is the trivial solution, and it is one if the solution is the best known solution.

[^2]: By trivial solution we mean the solution where each site is assigned exactly one route (which goes back and forth).

Evaluating this for CVRPLIB sample data yields the following graph.

```{r perf_scale_based_graph, echo=FALSE}
ggMarginal(
  merge(
    result,
    description,
    by = "group"
  ) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = n_site, y = clarke_wright_perf_xi,
               color = group_desc)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.5) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      name = "Best known vs. trivial",
      labels = scales::label_percent(),
      position = "left"
    ) +
    scale_x_continuous(
      name = "Number of demanding sites",
      position = "bottom"
    ) +
    scale_colour_discrete(name = NULL) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
    guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 3)),
  type = "boxplot",
  margins = "y",
  list(alpha = 0.6),
  groupFill = TRUE
)

```

The mean value over all problem instances is $\overline{\xi}=`r xi_mean`\%$.

## Relative deviation from best known solution

We can also simply measure the relative deviation of the Clarke-Wright cost to the best known cost, $$\rho := \frac{\gamma - \omega}{\gamma}\,,$$ which measures how much savings we miss by using the Clarke-Wright solution instead of the best known solution.

```{r perf_rel_graph, echo = FALSE}
ggMarginal(
  merge(
    result,
    description,
    by = "group"
  ) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = n_site, y = clarke_wright_perf_rho, color = group_desc)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.5) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      name = "Relative loss of savings",
      labels = scales::label_percent()
    ) +
    scale_x_continuous(
      name = "Number of demanding sites",
      position = "bottom"
    ) +
    scale_colour_discrete(name = NULL) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
    guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 3)),
  type = "boxplot",
  margins = "y",
  list(alpha = 0.6),
  groupFill = TRUE
)
```

The mean value over all problem instances is $\overline{\rho}=`r rho_mean`\%$, i.e. on average, we miss out on around $`r rho_mean`\%$ savings taking the Clarke-Wright solution compared to the best known one. For the instances derived from real problems (Loggi and ORTEC) it amounts to $`r rho_real_mean`\%$.

## Run time

The following graph shows the median run time of `clarke_wright_cvrplib()` for each instance, on an Intel® Xeon® CPU E3-1231 v3 \@ 3.40GHz.

```{r runtime_graph, echo = FALSE}
merge(
  result,
  description,
  by = "group"
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n_site, y = runtime, color = group_desc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Run time (in seconds)",
    labels = scales::label_number(suffix = "s")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "Number of demanding sites"
  ) +
  scale_colour_discrete(name = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 3))
```

The slowest of the instances with `r max(result$n_site)` sites takes around $`r runtime_ms(large)`$ ms.
